title: Silence turns a settlement figure into an Agreed Amount
content:
A.2.4.1.2.1.2.1 defines an Agreed Amount as one where "the Prime Agent does not post a Dispute Notice with respect to that amount within the period specified," and A.2.4.1.2.1.2.2 makes everything else a Disputed Amount. A.2.4.1.2.1.2.4 sets the window: a Dispute Notice must be posted as a reply to the Monthly Settlement Cycle Post "within five (5) calendar days of the posting of the Initial Calculation," and must "specify the errors in the Initial Calculation and the Prime's own calculation of the net amount."

Default-to-agreement is what makes a monthly cycle possible at all. The alternative — requiring affirmative sign-off from every Prime Agent — would let one unresponsive party stall settlement for everyone, and the calendar is tight: A.2.4.1.2.1.1 gives Operational Executor Agents seven days to post Initial Calculations and A.2.4.1.2.1.2 gives Core GovOps twelve days to post the Final Calculation, leaving little slack.

The burden this places on Primes is real. Each must independently verify its own numbers within five days, and the Dispute Notice bar is substantive — identifying errors and supplying a competing calculation, not merely objecting. A Prime without its own settlement accounting is effectively accepting whatever it is handed.

That asymmetry is sharpened by who prepares the figure. The Initial Calculation is produced by the Operational Executor Agent, which A.2.4.1.2.1.1.1 and A.2.4.1.2.1.3.3 confirm can itself be a payee — it flags Demand Side Primitive payments already made so they are "reimbursed to the Operational Executor Agent instead of being paid to the Prime Agent." The counterparty computing the number has a stake in it, and the five-day clock is the Prime's only structural protection.
description: A net amount in an Initial Calculation becomes Agreed unless the Prime Agent posts a Dispute Notice within five days, so non-response is consent and the dispute burden sits with the Prime.
